comments.author: fucklockjaw
comments.body:
Looks fun.  
Real question, are you vibing the whole thing or do you actually review and have it write decent code?

replies.author: Turbulent-Stretch881
replies.body:
The review part is right and it should stay. The second part is bilge.

I assure you any decent model can write better, more than "decent" code than any 1 individual, including you.

If you need me to explain the last part, maybe you should re-think whether tech is the right field for you. Not an insult, but a reality check.

replies.author: fucklockjaw
replies.body:
So if I blindly trust the output of something fallible and non-deterministic which is known for hallucinating and outputting objectively false information and unsecure code, this means I should rethink if tech is right for me?  

I just want to make sure I understand your comment.

replies.author: Turbulent-Stretch881
replies.body:
If you spent the same amount of time writing this than reading you'd see its mute, but here it goes again:

_The review part is right and it should stay_ - nobody is telling you to do anything blindly; but between than and scrutinizing everything with the monolith idea that _you are better_ (because you don't hallucinate apparently or have sub par output) than it or collective knowledge.

All the successful devs I knew lived in stackoverflow, discords, tech forums; because that's how/where they could _stay up to date_; _stay relevant_.

The attitude of "I know more, so I need to double check the output" that is flawed.

Its the same mentality of devs who think they're god's gift to software and anything less than have been written or audited by them is bad.

Here's an interesting take for you which instead of trying to fight people on reddit with the "let me see if I got this straight.." stance: start a new project with AI/vibe code, but do it in a language you don't know or understand - challenge it, work together, I'm sure you'll come out of it learning more than you would have had going in.

No. Its not perfect. 
But yes, it is much better _than any one developer/monolith_.

replies.author: fucklockjaw
replies.body:
I feel you have a real message in here but you ended your original comment in a very condescending way.  

I'm trying to understand. So if you're willing to explain I'm willing to listen. What exactly is it you're trying to say?  

All I asked is if OP reviews the code or not.

replies.author: Turbulent-Stretch881
replies.body:
You asked. Its going to be a long one.

And the moment you say "English is not my first language" probably half of this collapses: the main point though is tied with using the word "decent" (which _only_ becomes so if/when reviewed):

TL:DR: 

Current models produce _more than good_ code (let alone decent), so:

If the statement is even "decent code", then either:

Not dev; ignorance is bliss.

Dev; not keeping up to date with industry = sub par dev = this isn't the right industry (if we assume we should be doing better than sub par)

Am I right in saying that if you could define yourself on a scale of 1-10, 1 being Anti AI, 10 being in AI psychosis that you're somewhere around 3/10?

For me the right spectrum of people working in tech towards AI should be in the 7-8/10 range.

AI to tech is the equivalent of the synthesizer to music. When it came, you had adopters, you had haters, you had people on the fence.

But you know what's "worse" in my book? People (on both sides) that slam or hail something based on their sentiment towards it, but that in most cases, do not have enough expertise on the subject to actually base that sentiment on.

AI Models (Opus 4.6/7, Codex 5.3) are _more than capable_ to deliver _decent_ code. More than decent in fact. With/out review. Obviously _with_ is preferred. But "decent" was a conversation we were having in 2025, not now.

It is not perfect. Nothing is. If your PM comes asking for "bug free code" or "test exhaustively" or the whole analogy of delivering with 9 women and 1 month  instead of 1 in 9; these are all industry standard analogies/I suggest to look em up if you want to know the scenarios: it doesn't matter if it is AI or employee of the month X. Sometimes its a matter of expectations.

The likelihood of these models having errors are likely less than _you_ or any one/small group of devs thinking they are.

These models/where we got today are based on training it would take you years to go through, by people with both academic backgrounds (PHDs/million dollar contracts), companies worth billions, testing, maintaining, improving their product. I acknowledge that. Regardless of the ego of how good I think I am.

Just because you're human, writing code like a human doesn't make it inherently "better".

The fact that you add the "decent" statement it directly points to the question:

_"What does he mean, decent...? Does he not use these models? REGARDLESS OF VIBE CODING, even simply requesting a pull request with updates/hardening: I am sure your codebase will have 3-4 issues you wouldn't have known about or seen. It could simply be that they became common standard 1 month ago, you still would not have been lagging behind. 

So if today, you work in tech, and do not have fundamental knowledge of what "decent" code they are producing, which the only valid reason I can think of is; you do not use them in your workflow ("I used it a year ago and it was bad" is not a valid answer. Neither is free ChatGpt or Free gemini, or worse, Copilot) - then yes, I re-iterate my point: tech might not be the right industry for that case in that scenario.

Because that's one of the qualities which make a _good_ developer apart from the rest/salaried engineers (which will be phased out) - they know they need to keep up to date, learning new tech, collaborate, _adopt new tools_. 

So TL:DR: 

Current models produce _more than good_ code (let alone decent), so:

If the statement is even "decent code", then either:

Not dev; ignorance is bliss.

Dev; not keeping up to date with industry = sub par dev = this isn't the right industry (if we assume we should be doing better than sub par).

So, if you made it this far, I would bet $1 that you work in tech, do not use AI (other than free gemini/chatgpt/company Copilot license), or maybe tried claude one time long ago, but know who does, and maybe they are too loud about it and "overuse it" in your mind, to the point that you see them as bad devs because they are risking bad hallucinations or security issues so think that since you need to review it yourself, then you might as well write it yourself in the first place...

I know I got part of it right for sure.

Thing is, those devs using AI heavily are producing 2x more bugs (from hallucinations /security) than you, but are also outputting 10x more code; error rate is also lower.

Or better, offset _certain_ type of code to it - maybe you can make scripts, better devops deployment pipelines, even general "grunt" work to free up more of your time which you could dedicate to things which require further attention.

The point is; we're past decent. And if you don't know that and you work in tech, you're not using it or is familiar enough with it; and to me, in this industry, even from an evaluating standpoint to keep up to date, deep understanding of latest tech is fundamental.

Because just like those who decided to not adopt or learn enough about synthesizers in the 80s or think might as well play the instrument instead of sampling it altogether still worked.. but those who did were better, best of both words, some even with better opportunities.

Get yourself codex 5.3 or opus4.6+ and see what a developer _and_ these models produce. Spend money. Even if you have to rotate a different subscription every month. But get educated. Because if you are not, in this industry (like others, but more frequently in this one), someone else will. And he/she _will_ eat your lunch.

Final point; nobody owes you to be "nice" to you on the internet. But the best you can get is actually an unfiltered take. You had it here.
